projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Clarence Francis Sindy was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Clarence Francis Sindy. His last name was originally Sindodecker (phonetic). Clarence served in the U.S. Army with the 66th Signal Battalion. He served in the ETO at Pacific Theater. I'm Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Sindy's home in Willoughby, Ohio, on March 16th, 2004. Clarence was 82 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Cleveland, Ohio. I had just graduated from Collinwood High School in January, and I applied for a job at General Electric as a machinist apprentice. That all happened in January 1941.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. It was a Sunday. I remember that distinctly. I'll never forget the president and the speech he made about the dastardly act that happened at Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm. What was your personal reaction to that news?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: A couple days later, my father and I went up and registered for the draft.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: It was a reaction of, "What can I do to help?"

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How old was your father?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: He was about 39 at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did he ever serve --

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He served in World War I. In fact, he was in the Air Force -- the Air Corps in World War I and helped demolish a lot of old DeHavillands and World War I biplanes. I remember pictures of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: They didn't call him in World War II?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: No, no. Thank goodness.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So let's see. We have you enlisted in the summer of '42. Did you do anything for the war effort before that time, before you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: I joined the Red Cross. I remember that and giving blood. But that was the only thing that I can remember actually doing. And because my dad had been in the Air Force or the Air Corps -- people call it the Air Force now, but prior to '46 it was the Air Corps. And it was interesting in the fact that I ended up going to school at Fort Monmouth, New Jersey, and we went to school in hangars from the first World War, because the Air Corps was part of the Signal Corps. They were used as observation planes so -- and fighters, naturally, but not too many people remember World War I anymore.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I didn't realize the Air Corps is basically part of the Signal Corps --

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: -- not necessarily a fighting tool at that point.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Originally they were observation.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So did you enlist or were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: I enlisted, and my mother was very concerned about that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And that was June of '42?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. My dad, he just stood back and never said a word.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you think he was proud?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: He was proud but unhappy about the situation.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you went off to basic training, was it a tough adjustment to be there with the guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yes, especially the guys from Brooklyn. I couldn't understand them. And we had some fellows from Chicago. One of the guys didn't even speak English. All German. We told him we were going to put him in the front lines. In fact, to help him understand English better, they made him like a permanent CQ, and he would catch you doing something that you weren't supposed to do, and he'd say, "I turn your ass in the _______." That was the first phrase that he could really get out in English.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What else can you tell me about basic training?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: You know, I don't really remember it too much, because it went so fast, and it was so different than civilian life.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: It was interesting, but 25-mile hikes, that's -- that can get to you.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Now, did you say you did some of your training at Fort Monmouth?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah, that was -- When I enlisted, I enlisted in the Air Corps. I got to Camp Crowder because I was taking double E at Fen (phonetic), and they put me in the Signal Corps because they had just opened up Camp Crowder. We were some of the first troops in there. So I'm talking to the captain one day, and I told him I had enlisted in the Air Corps, and they put me in the Signal Corps. "How come?" He said, "Well, if you're so damned smart, go over and take the cadet test." So I took the cadet test, and it took about six or seven months after I passed the test before I went to the Air Corps. And during that time I went through all of the schools that they had at Camp Crowder, all the signal schools as far as wire was concerned.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you were trained in the Signal Corps in the meantime?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. It was very good training too. They had a lot of cadre from Bell Telephone. In fact, in our company, if you weren't a Bell Telephone man, you had a hard time getting a promotion. And there was reason for it. Of course, we couldn't see that at the time since we were foreigners, so to speak.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So now, eventually, you did end up in the Army Air Corps?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. After that six or seven months interim at Camp Crowder, they put us on a train one day. There were 90 of us all together, and we ended up going all the way to Denver from Missouri and back to Tennessee, Nashville, Tennessee, for classification center. And they spend three days looking at your eyeballs and everything else to make sure you could see and your body was in pretty good shape. And after passing the physical they sent us to Maxwell Field, Alabama, and there we had preflight. And the thing I remember most about Maxwell Field was I had the wife down for our graduation dance, and Glenn Miller played -- they were the orchestra. He was stationed at Maxwell Field. Very beautiful band.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything specific about that show?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. He played Tuxedo Junction and -- oh, there were a half dozen -- there was a song about the moon.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Midnight Serenade?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah, Midnight Serenade. It was just beautiful.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You didn't get a chance to see or get up close with Glenn Miller any time?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you talk to him?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Well, he's playing in the band, and he comes over and shakes hands with the fellows in the front dance area, and it really hurt, because we were in Fecamp, France, Camp Lucky Strike, waiting to go up to relieve the guys from the Bulge, and we found out that his plane had disappeared. And it was like losing a family friend. He was a nice little _______.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was that the reaction of a lot of the guys?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. I never heard anybody say anything detrimental about Glenn Miller. I guess he was a very dedicated individual as far as music was concerned, and you had to play it right or you weren't around.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So what were you trained as in the Army Air Corps?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: I was trained as a pilot. And after Maxwell Field, we went to Lafayette, Louisiana, for primary, and after primary we went to Greenwood, Mississippi. What a place that was. There wasn't a beer joint in town, but outside of town there was a big circle of places of ill repute, so to speak. I washed out after about 120 hours at Greenwood, Mississippi. I happened to overshoot the field one day when the medical observer was there, and he gave three of us a maytag the next day.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What's a maytag?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Maytag, that's a washout. And he said I had bad depth perception. And I couldn't understand that, naturally, being examined and everything. And it kind of soured me on the Air Corps, because I wanted to be able to fly. But I went back to the Signal Corps. So -- I didn't want anything to do -- they wanted to put me in bombardier school, and I said, "No, I'd rather go back to my old outfit." They were getting ready to go overseas at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You chose to either fly or forget about it?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: When you're washed out, the only way you can fly is somebody else flying behind you.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You had no desire to be a crew member --

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: No. You know, you're 21 years old, and it's the first big defeat of your life, and you kind of -- well, you're ignorant of life, so to speak, at that stage.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So then it was back to Signal Corps?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. I went to the 217 Signal -- Signal Company where I had been before I went to the Air Corps, but they were just ready to go overseas, and I didn't have enough time to take all the examinations before you went overseas. You had a -- There was a physical thing, and you just had to do it before you went overseas. And consequently, they cadried me into the 99th Signal Battalion, which of all things was desert maneuvers. And if you've never eaten soup with sand in it, you can go to a desert maneuver sometime. Then they got to the point where they were going to go overseas, and I guess one of the last things you do is get rid of the people you don't want, and I -- because I had such little time with the outfit, I was cadried into the 66th Signal Battalion, which was just starting up at Camp Crowder. From there we went on winter maneuvers. Now, winter maneuvers is quite different than desert maneuvers. We were freezing our everything off. And I'll never -- I'll never forget coming back from chow one time, and Britsky, one of the members of our organization, I see him on a pile of snow about six feet high, and he's got his clothes off on a blanket, and he's shaving himself. I said, "My God, Britsky! What are you doing, freezing to death?" He said, "Uh, I got a dose of crabs at Merton's." In Nashville, they had a place where we all went to take a hot bath. It was a Turkish bath outfit. He said, "I got a dose of crabs, and they won't accept me in the medical tent until I shave all my hair off." He was built like a gorilla anyway. I really sympathized with him. From winter maneuvers, we went back to Fort Riley, Kansas, and they sent me to school at Fort Monmouth for about three or four months. I came out of there with a wire chief MOS. I forget the number of it -- 263, or something like that. And then we went to Camp Shanks, New York. They put us on a ship. I remember we left Pier 59 and sailed past the Statue of Liberty, a kind of tearful time, wondering if we'd ever get back. This was a 100-ship convoy that we were on, and we ended up in --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When was that? Let's see. That was in -- I'm trying to find that. Oh, it looks like December of '44.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That would have been the crossing?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was that crossing like?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: It was a 100-ship convoy, and there was ten ships, and they were all zigzagging and everything else. And about three days, we were -- three days to get to South Hampton. About 6:00 o'clock at night, our sister ship that was right beside us and that was the end of the convoy was torpedoed by a German submarine, and there was a lot of hubbub aboard ship. We were just coming back from chow, and those of us who had seen it were very perturbed and talking about seeing a psychiatrist. That's when there weren't any around. Anyway, down in the fifth hull they had about 500 black soldiers, and they all came up out of the fifth hull. Now that's the lowest part of the ship, and the MPs were trying to get them to go back down. I'll never forget this one fellow. Wide-eyed, he looked at the MP, he said, "You can get your .45 out and shoot me right between the eyes, but I'm not going back to that number five hull," and they stayed up on board ship until we got into South Hampton. And then they loaded us on LTTs.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: LSTs?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: LSTs, yeah, yeah. The Navy, they had a lot of initials, WPA, and all that stuff. And we landed at LaHavre and went to Camp Lucky Strike in France. I guess we were waiting to get shipped up around where the Bulge had been. Thank goodness the Bulge was over by then.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were they considering putting you in the infantry at that point, at the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: No. We had -- That never came up. That's a good point. I'm glad I wasn't in the infantry, because those poor guys -- you know, you think you had a hard time, but it was nothing compared to what those poor guys went through. They shipped us -- Just at our platoon, our water platoon was shipped up to Bad Godesberg, and we set up three or four -- four or five switching centrals. And this was all -- we were like corps headquarters for the -- It wasn't the third Army. First Army, I think it was. I remember the 101st Airborne and the 87th. They were -- they were rough -- There were a lot of rough kids in there from Texas. Talk about being rough, they were really rough. The only way we could get into Fecamp was they had what they called the Red Ball Express, and some of the trucks were hauling gravel from the shore back to the camp, and they were trying to make a place where the aircraft could land. And we jumped on this truck to go into Fecamp, and when we got off the truck, I was with a fellow from the 101st, a little guy from Texas, and when we got off the truck, why he yells out to the colored driver, he says, "Thank you, boy." And the colored driver, a big, big kid, sticks his head out of the door and he says, "Hey, I'm not a boy. I'm a man just like the rest of you guys." And the kid from Texas takes out his .45 and shoots him right between the eyes. I'll never forget that in my life. And when I hear somebody say something about prejudice, that always comes back to my mind. Horrible. But I skedaddled out of there real quick, because I didn't want him to use the damn thing on me. It was just amazing. I'd never seen anything like that. Well, how bad can you be?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did they ever reprimand him, put him in jail, whatever?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Well, we were on the way to Bad Godesberg so I never --

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You never heard what happened to him?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: I never heard what happened to him. But it really gets to you when something like that happens. You know, it burns a place in your mind. From -- After we got the water center set up, I guess they thought McArthur needed us, and they bundled us up, and for three days we drove in trucks to Marseille, France. We were set up in a camp just outside of Ecques. Marseille is interesting in the fact that it was the first place on the continent that the Greeks in 800 BC had a colony. They set up a colony in Sicily, and then they set up a colony in Marseille, France. They had a museum in Ecques. All it was was chastity belts. The French are different -- different people. They have different ways of looking at things. I get along with them, because I get in a conversation about Lafayette winning the war for the Americans during the revolution. And 59 days after we got on the boat, we got off at a little town in the north of Manila, Dagupan. Dagupan was a -- it was a home of mosquitos, I believe. And then they shipped us down to Tarlac. By that time we were attached to the 25th Division for rations and so forth, and then they put us on LSTs and sent us to Japan. We sailed up the shore of Japan to Nagoya and, as we looked up, the cliffs were similar to what you see on the West Coast of the United States, and you could see these airplanes and the zeros. They had ropes around the rear of the plane, and they were tied to trees, and they would rev -- rev the plane up, and they would chop the ropes, and the planes didn't need a runway. And this was a Kamikaze setup that they had. So when I got home, I voted for Harry S. Truman, because he actually saved our lives. Whether -- Democrats or Republicans argue about it, but if it hadn't have been for his saying to drop the bombs, why we wouldn't be here, because most of the people that would attack something like that would have been dead.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Now, were you in the Philippines when they dropped the bombs?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Could you comprehend what that was --

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: No, no. We didn't have the faintest idea what an atomic bomb was.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Any wild celebrations when VJ day did come?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. Things can't be too wild when all you can drink is water, and it tastes like chlorine. But it was interesting. In December when I left Marseille, I had 173 points, I think, and they were leaving them out with 100 points. But they claimed they needed wire people in the Philippines, so we were fortunate in getting a 59-day trip to the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about that particular trip, any rough weather or anything that you ran into?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: We were very fortunate. The only thing I can really remember is laying in the Kwajalein. And after you're at sea for a while, when you see palm trees growing out of the ocean, it's a beautiful scene. And there must have been 100 ships laying off Kwajalein to get stores, and I figured, Well, the next day we should have pretty good food. So Patsy Maggiore, Patsy NMI Maggiore, no middle initial, he was from Pittsburg, and he was our sergeant in charge of trucks and everything. He weighed about 240 pounds when we got on the ship in Marseille, and at the time this happened he must have weighed 160, because he couldn't eat at all. He couldn't keep anything down. He got seasick walking on board ship, he had it so bad. I guess it's the inner ear or something. Anyway, poor Patsy. I said, "Come on. Let's go eat chow. They should have good breakfast." So we go get in a chow line. What do they have? Fish and beans and a big red apple. The apple was the only thing out of the new stores. The fish and beans were from the old stores. So we ate the breakfast, and we bite into the apple. On the way up, we're standing on the edge of the ship, and poor Maggiore looks at the waves and gets seasick, and everything came back to me. And I know why they call it an Adam's apple, because that apple was stuck in my throat for a week. Poor Patsy. He couldn't eat. He had a heck of a time. In fact, I wonder how he ever got home.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How long were you in Japan?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Not too long. I think it was from September to December.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you have any encounters with the Japanese people there?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: The only encounter we had -- The second day we were in Nagoya -- Nagoya was all bombed out. They used the thermal bombs, and you'd see gas lines sticking up out of the ground where houses used to be. Of course, most of their houses were very fragile anyway. We're driving down the street -- We're going into Nagoya to pick up some wire, we're driving down the street, and out of nowhere comes this great big Japanese lorry. And it comes right in front of us, and we bang into it with one of these 4x4s. What it was, it was an electrical car. They were putting up new electricity lines, and out of the back of this lorry comes 30 Japanese, and they're all "bla-bla-bla" in Japanese. It was like watching all those clowns get out of a Volkswagen. I'll never forget that. The only other incident I had was sampling some of the Japanese rice whiskey. They give it to you hot. They give it to you out of a teapot. Very -- very intoxicating.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was your specific job with the Signal Corps?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: I was a water chief. We had a platoon of guys, and our job was to set up switching centrals. We had an old 501-B Kellogg switchboard in a 2-1/2 ton truck with wire lines and a wire setup, and we would send -- take that to corps headquarters and set up 25 to 30 phones for corps headquarters. And this is what we did in _______ and Liege, the Netherlands. It was setting up field switchboards.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When did you finally get home?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: January of '46. I went back to work at General Electric, and they were on strike. So my brother-in-law got me a job working for the architect firm that he worked in, and that lasted for about a month. And then I went back to GE when the strike was over.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you finally did get back to the States, how long had it been since you had seen your family, your wife?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Over a year.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was the reunion like when you saw her?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Well, I remember she had cold feet. Of course, we had had a son by then, and he couldn't figure me out. This guy comes in the house and all of a sudden tells the kid what to do, and the kid isn't used to that gruff voice and so forth. It was interesting. As you look back on it, you can see these things, but at the time, why, stupidity ruled.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: How old was he when you came back?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: He was almost two years old, just sitting up and eating. And I remember we took him to a restaurant one time, and he had his first real solid meal. And the way he went into the potatoes and gravy, it was funny watching him.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of mail call when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Not too much. We didn't get too many -- too much mail overseas, because we were hither and yon all the time. But there was nothing more welcome than a letter from home. I wish I had saved some of the mail. I didn't save anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you write much back home?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: I tried to write each day. I wasn't always able to do it, but I tried.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: When you got overseas, did you get much entertainment?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The one I remember most is with about 80,000 people outside of Marseille, France. They had a natural amphitheater. I don't know if it was originally built by the Romans or not, because I wasn't interested in that. I was interested in Bob Hope. And he had -- Bob Hope and the guy with a mustache.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Jerry Colonna?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Jerry Colonna. Oh my God. And then they had a little female singer.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Possibly Frances Langford?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Frances Langford. She'd never fall on her nose. You can imagine 80,000 GIs watching something like that. Bob Hope was a terrific guy, a Cleveland boy, by the way.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything specific at all about that show?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: No, not very much except Jerry Colonna and Bob Hope and Frances Langford. And Frances Langford had a heck of a voice. She could really knock out a song.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you get a good seat?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: I was about 400 rows back.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Out of 80,000, that doesn't sound bad.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: But they had a good PA system, and you could hear everything that was going on. In fact, you even heard the things that you weren't supposed to hear.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies in the service?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. In fact, I just got a letter from -- our 66th Signal reunion that's going to take place in July and August in -- where the heck is it -- west of Chicago. Iola is it? Is it Iola?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That sounds right.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Yeah. We get together each year. Each year there's less of us. Last year I imagine there was 25 or 30. They've all got fat, lost their hairs. Some of them can't walk too well. We're getting old.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies in your outfit back during the wars?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. We lost most of them to stupidity. We had one guy that we sent to Czechoslovakia. He was our best guy in setting up lines for teletype, and he was -- They had a lot of steel poles in Czechoslovakia. That's not steel Pollacks. These are steel telephone poles. He was up on a pole and went across the wrong wire, and it electrocuted him. So we went up to pick him up. We were going to bring him back to a burial spot in the Netherlands, Andover, I believe it was, and we stopped at a bar to get a beer before we took off. And we're sitting there, and this Russian comes in, parks his Jeep right out in front. He comes in and he has a vodka. And I asked him, "What do you think of that American Jeep?" He says, "No American. Ruskie Jeep." So we went out, and in the glove compartment they had a -- it must have been a 30-page unit on how to drive the Jeep and so forth, and how to take care of it. It was all in Russian, all except the front piece that said "Manufactured by Ford Motor Company, Dearborn, Michigan." He put it back in the glove compartment, took off. He didn't say a word. I don't believe that the Russians appreciated the Americans too much, because there was a -- a difference in looking at life between the two. The Russians were very -- There were a lot of Russians in Germany that were prisoners of war, and a lot of women too, women -- Polish and Russian. Very gruff people. I guess they -- they saw the worst of the whole war, and we didn't appreciate what we saw. You look at it from different eyeballs.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What did you think about your experiences during the war? Does one particular vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: The only one I can really remember was when I was in the Air Corps, we finished primary, and Greenwood, Mississippi was filled up because the bad weather that they had. The first part of the alphabet -- These are 99 guys in the squadron. The first part of the alphabet got 30-day furlough. The second part went to gunnery school. Well, S is in the second part of the alphabet, so we went to Laredo, Texas. Talk about being hot. That was hotter than the desert was, and we're not -- they had us in this -- well, it was a valley, like. I think they called it Aurora or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Arroyo?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Arroyo. We had the 50-millimeter set up on one side and the targets on the other side, and we were just ready to start shooting, and this sergeant comes down in a Jeep, and he in very undiplomatic language told us to get the hell up the side of the valley, because there was a flash flood coming down. And I never seen anything like this. An eight-foot wave of water comes down, and because the valley floor was like concrete, it became a conduit, and it just rushed by, and it took the Jeep with it. And if it hadn't have been for him, we would have had a lot of trouble. That was the closest I think I came. Our granddaughter now lives in San Antonio, not too far from Laredo. In fact, every time I think about her down in San Antonio, I think about Laredo, Texas. Well, that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: That's four years of joy and education.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you certainly appreciated your time in the service?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Very much so, yeah. We had some wonderful individuals, and I can't wait to see them in July.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Um-hmm.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Some of them, the ones that are left. In fact, these guys in this picture of the fellows in primary, there's only two left. This guy died of trench mouth, of all things, and two of them were shot over Germany. And these two here were shot over in Japan. So -- and I don't know what happened to him. He passed away too.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So --

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: But old Solsgaver (phonetic) and I are the only ones left out of that group of nine kids.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Before I forget, I don't think we got the story on tape about the beer. I think that was before I started the tape, right?

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: The beer?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: About the guy in Panama.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Oh, I thought we did.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: I think it was before I started the tape rolling.

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell that, and I'll make sure I put that on --

sp.speaker: Clarence Francis Sindy
sp.p: Well, Britsky was formerly a brew master down in Panama, Panama City, and when we stopped there on the way to the Philippines, they let us off the ship for a day so we could find out what terra firma was. And Britsky said, "Let's go over to the brewery where I was brew master, and I'll show you around." We go over, and the new brew master, the first thing he tells Britsky is, "I'm making 10,000 bucks a year." And Britsky, when he was brought into the service, was making 7,000. You could see him turn red, and the brew master realized he had a faux pas there, so he gives us a couple cases of beer and a couple bottles of whiskey. I forget what the heck they were. Southern Comfort, that was it, which was a sweet whiskey. We go back to the barracks where we were stationed and started playing poker, and about halfway through the beer, one of the guys notices on the beer that it was 23 proof. You never saw guys get so drunk in all your life, just like that. Even Britsky got stoned. (END OF CD.)
